content: 1. Patients presenting with symptoms of genital or anal ulcers should be reviewed after one week if symptoms persist or recur. Treatment should be guided by test results available on the same day. If testing is unavailable, treatment for herpes simplex virus (HSV) and syphilis should be initiated empirically. 2. Testing for HIV and syphilis, along with other preventive services, should be offered to individuals with genital ulcer symptoms. If laboratory capacity is limited or unavailable, clinical diagnosis and syndromic management should be employed. 3. If a sore or ulcer is present, and the ulcer is vesicular or there is a history of recurrent ulcers at the same site, treatment for HSV and syphilis should be provided. This approach is based on evidence of moderate to high certainty regarding the sensitivity and specificity of clinical diagnosis for sexually transmitted infections (STIs) associated with anogenital ulcers. 4. For syphilis, which accounts for 5–10% of anogenital ulcers, clinical diagnosis has a sensitivity of 64% and specificity of 84%. In a cohort of 100 individuals with ulcers, 2–4 cases of syphilis may be missed, and 14–15 individuals may be falsely diagnosed and unnecessarily treated. Treating all 100 individuals empirically for syphilis would prevent missed cases but result in 90–95 unnecessary treatments. 5. Molecular assays, which are highly sensitive and specific, can reduce unnecessary treatments and missed cases. However, these tests may be costly and inaccessible in some settings. The WHO recommends treating all ulcers for syphilis in settings with limited testing capacity, as the long-term consequences of missed syphilis cases outweigh the costs of unnecessary treatment. 6. For HSV, which accounts for 30–70% of anogenital ulcers, clinical diagnosis has a sensitivity of 40% and specificity of 88%. In a cohort of 100 individuals, 18–42 cases of HSV may be missed, and 4–8 individuals may be unnecessarily treated. Empirically treating all 100 individuals for HSV would result in 30–70 unnecessary treatments, but the cost of treatment is relatively low. 7. The WHO suggests treating all genital ulcers for HSV in settings with limited laboratory capacity to improve quality of life and reduce discomfort for symptomatic individuals. This approach is considered feasible, cost-effective, and equitable. 8. The prevalence of chancroid has decreased globally, and clinical diagnosis for chancroid results in minimal missed cases but significant unnecessary treatments. The WHO recommends no treatment for chancroid unless surveillance indicates emerging cases. 9. For lymphogranuloma venereum (LGV), no evidence exists regarding the cost-benefit of clinical diagnosis. Testing for LGV should depend on the prevalence of cases, and treatment should only be initiated if a test is positive. 10. Syndromic management of genital ulcer disease should include treatment for syphilis (unless treated within the past three months) and HSV. Suppressive therapy is recommended for individuals with frequent or severe recurrent ulcers, with reassessment after one year to determine whether to continue or switch to episodic treatment. 11. For individuals living with HIV or immunosuppressed patients, dose adjustments for valaciclovir and famciclovir are recommended, but not for acyclovir. For recurrent episodes, valaciclovir 500 mg is recommended for five days, and famciclovir 500 mg twice daily for five days. For suppressive therapy, valaciclovir 500 mg twice daily and famciclovir 500 mg twice daily are recommended. 12. Penicillin-allergic individuals should be treated with effective alternatives for syphilis, such as doxycycline or erythromycin. However, erythromycin does not cross the placental barrier completely, so newborns of treated pregnant women require treatment after delivery. 13. Anorectal infections are prevalent among men who have sex with men, female sex workers, transgender individuals, and women engaging in receptive anal intercourse. These infections can involve the anus, rectum, or colon and may present with symptoms such as pain, itching, discharge, bleeding, or tenesmus. Asymptomatic infections are also common. 14. High-risk sexual practices associated with anorectal infections include receptive anal sex, oro-anal contact, fisting, fingering, unprotected external penile-anal contact, partial anal penetration, and sharing sex toys. 15. Examination for anal infections should include external inspection and, where available, anoscopy. In asymptomatic cases, anoscopy with Gram-stained smear and leukocyte count may help screen for STIs. However, anoscopy is often unavailable in primary care settings, and external examination may be the only practical option. 16. For anorectal discharge, molecular assays (NAAT) using self-collected or clinician-collected swabs are recommended to confirm or exclude infections with Neisseria gonorrhoeae and Chlamydia trachomatis. If molecular testing is unavailable, empirical treatment for these infections is suggested. 17. Empirical treatment for HSV should be added if anorectal pain is present. If laboratory capacity is limited, individuals with persistent anorectal discharge should be referred to centers with diagnostic capabilities for gonorrhea, chlamydia (including LGV serovars), and Mycoplasma genitalium. 18. Syndromic management of anorectal discharge has moderate harm and minor benefits compared to molecular testing or treating all individuals empirically. Treating everyone with anorectal discharge for gonorrhea and chlamydia ensures no cases are missed but results in high rates of unnecessary treatment. 19. Research is needed to validate laboratory tests for rectal specimens and treatment options for anorectal infections. Surveillance data on asymptomatic syphilis among high-risk populations can help adapt management guidelines to include syphilis treatment for those at risk. 20. The WHO recommends molecular testing for anorectal infections where feasible, as it leads to the most accurate treatment. In settings without molecular testing, treating all individuals with anorectal discharge is a feasible and cost-effective alternative.
